course_description: Historical Archaeology examines what the archaeology of the recent past reveals about the making of the modern world. The course concentrates on the phenomena that have defined the last few centuries: colonialism, capitalism, industrialisation and the experiences of marginalised peoples, and on the distinctive methods historical archaeologists use to study them. Weekly case studies range across shipwrecks, Indigenous entanglements with colonial systems, illicit and clandestine behaviours, and the biographies of everyday objects, giving students a broad comparative view of how material evidence and the documentary record can be brought into productive tension. The course pairs this thematic breadth with hands-on practical training. Through laboratory practicals, students learn to identify, date and interpret common classes of historical artefacts found in Australian archaeological contexts. Because historical archaeology works at the interface of past and present, the course also asks how and why this evidence is communicated to wider audiences.

learning_outcomes.description: Interpret human activity at a range of scales, from individual sites to broader processes such as colonialism and capitalism
Apply key historical archaeological theory and method to research problems, drawing on diverse sources of evidence
Describe the political, ethical and professional frameworks that shape how historical archaeology is practised
Identify and record the characteristics for common classes of artefacts found in Australian historical archaeological contexts

assessment_details.title: Cemetery Report
assessment_details.task_description: For this assignment you will record data for 12 historical burial memorials from one cemetery and prepare a report that thematically discusses the results. The list of eligible cemeteries is: Alberton Bald Hills Balmoral Beenleigh Bethania Brookfield Caboolture Cleveland Dunwich Eagleby Ipswich Logan Village Nudgee Catholic Nundah South Brisbane (Dutton Park) Southport Toowong To complete this assessment, you will: Select a cemetery from the above list. Visit the cemetery (take means to record the memorials, a camera and a tape measure). Identify pre-WWI (pre-1914) burial memorials in the cemetery. These may be in one area or across the cemetery. Select twelve memorials for this study that have a range of variables suitable for identifying a pattern. Record the details of each memorial. You can use the recording form provided on Blackboard, or create your own form (such as excel spreadsheet or notebook). You should fill in every section of the form or include the same information in another format. Take at least one photo of each memorial and at least one photo of yourself at the cemetery. Please be respectful while you are recording and photographing memorials. Prepare a concise report that includes: A. A summary of the data collected for the 12 burial memorials. B. Presentation of one pattern you observed across the memorials, relating to variables such as age, sex, year of death or the grave materials. C. Discussion of this pattern in relation to a theme and relevant historical archaeological theory. D. An appendix of your record form/s and photographs of each memorial. The word limit for the report is 2500 words, including tables and in-text references, but not including appendices and your reference list. This is a maximum word count (not +/- 10%); if you can meet the report requirements more concisely, it is acceptable to submit a report with a shorter word limit. 8. Submit your completed report via the Turnitin submission portal. Additional guiding information about selecting and recording memorials, and preparing the report will be supplied in the ‘Assessment’ folder in Blackboard and discussed during lectures (Weeks 3 and 4). Marking criteria: Criteria including rubrics are available in the ‘Assessments’ folder on the course Blackboard site. AI Use: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which AI may provide limited support and guidance. A failure to reference AI use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct Policy. Students may be required to complete an AI usage declaration and submit it with their assessment. Additional resources are available through UQ AI Student Hub . learning_activities.topic: What is historical archaeology? An introduction to historical and contemporary archaeology and where they sit within the broader discipline. (Course and assessment overview is provided separately on Blackboard.) Learning outcomes: L01, L03
Evidence in historical archaeology What counts as evidence for historical archaeologists, and how this shapes the methods we use. Learning outcomes: L02, L04

Working with artefacts Get hands-on with the core methods historical archaeologists use to turn artefacts into interpretation. This foundational practical builds the handling, recording and analytical skills you'll draw on in every practical that follows. Learning outcomes: L02, L04
Themes and theory in historical archaeology A tour through key theoretical lenses and themes historical archaeologists use to interpret the archaeological record. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Cemetery studies Why and how historical archaeologists study cemeteries, with a look at the Old Sydney Burial Ground, isotopic analysis, and what doing this kind of work looked like in 1970s Australia! Sets up the cemetery assignment. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Ceramic artefacts Learn to identify, characterise and date historical ceramics. Through hands-on exercises with 19th- and 20th-century material, you'll practise the work-related skills used by professional historical archaeologists and heritage consultants when analysing ceramic assemblages. Learning outcomes: L04
Interconnected networks Using the archaeological record to trace capitalism and global trade, explored through the successive waves of colonisation on Norfolk Island. Learning outcomes: L01, L03
Colonialism and its entanglements How colonial archaeology reveals the entangled relationships between peoples, using case studies from the Cape York Peninsula. Learning outcomes: L01, L03

Glass artefacts An introduction to the historical archaeological analysis of glass, including identification, manufacturing techniques and dating methods. Through practical exercises with 19th- and 20th-century glass artefacts, you'll build the work-related skills used to interpret glass assemblages from historical sites. Learning outcomes: L04

Cultural complexity in the historical period Reading social stratification, gender, ethnicity and age through material culture, with a focus on Point Puer, lutruwita/Tasmania, a prison for convict children. Learning outcomes: L01, L02
Power How the archaeological record reveals inequality and power relations, explored through plantation landscapes. Learning outcomes: L01, L03

Metals, plastics and building materials Identification, manufacture and dating of metal, plastic and building material artefacts. Hands-on exercises let you practise the work-related skills needed to interpret 19th- and 20th-century objects in these material categories. Learning outcomes: L04

Stratigraphy and analysis Historical archaeology often involves highly stratified sites and complex stratigraphic relationships. This week we'll look more closely at how analysis in historical archaeology employs method and theory for stratigraphy-based analysis. Learning outcomes: L02
Mid Semester Break

Institutions and ideology What institutions are, why they emerged in the modern world, and how archaeology captures both institutional agendas and lived experience — using a site that shifted from convict lumber yard to asylum. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Consolidating your practical skills This week we will consolidate our knowledge of historical artefacts with some structured exercises, as well as spending time preparing for the practical exam. Learning outcomes: L04
Hidden worlds Illicit behaviour and the social forces shaping it, through a secret cache of artefacts found at the Royal Derwent Hospital, lutruwita/Tasmania.. Learning outcomes: L01, L02
In-class artefact practical exam (Assessment) The exam will occur in a 1-hour timeslot within the timetabled class. Learning outcomes: L04
Urban historical archaeology Archaeology in and of the city, using Melbourne's 'Little Lon', the idea of the 'slum', and artefacts recovered from cesspits. Learning outcomes: L01, L03

Archaeology in the present What an archaeology of/for the present looks like, via the Transit Van Project and a recent Australian vehicle archaeology study, and a return to historical archaeology's relevance today. Learning outcomes: L03
